name: Pericardial effusion
summary: Fluid in the pericardial space. On echo it is a dark, echo-free space between the heart and the bright parietal pericardium.
findings: In the parasternal long axis, look for a dark space between the inferolateral wall and the bright pericardial line.
Follow the space toward the left atrium and check that it passes in front of the descending aorta.
Check whether fluid also lies in front of the RV. Small effusions usually collect behind the heart first, while larger ones surround it.
Size the effusion by its widest echo-free space at end-diastole. The ESC grades it as mild under 10 mm, moderate 10 to 20 mm and large over 20 mm.
Confirm in the subcostal and apical views, which show fluid around the RV and the right atrium.
Note strands, clot or debris in the fluid, which suggest an inflammatory or bloody effusion rather than a simple one.
Finish by looking for chamber collapse, which raises the question of tamponade.
significance: How fast fluid collects matters as much as how much there is. A small effusion that builds quickly can cause tamponade, while a large chronic one may be well tolerated.
pearls: Pericardial fluid tracks in front of the descending aorta in the long axis. Left pleural fluid stays behind it.
A dark space seen only in front of the RV is often epicardial fat, which looks slightly speckled and moves with the heart.
Measure at end-diastole so that serial studies can be compared.
sources: Adler Y et al. 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases. Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921-2964. PMID 26320112.
Klein AL et al. ASE clinical recommendations for multimodality cardiovascular imaging of patients with pericardial disease. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013;26:965-1012. PMID 23998693.
Mitchell C et al. Guidelines for Performing a Comprehensive Transthoracic Echocardiographic Examination in Adults. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2019;32:1-64. PMID 30282592.

name: Cardiac tamponade
summary: A clinical diagnosis of circulatory compromise caused by pericardial fluid compressing the heart. Echo does not make the diagnosis alone, but it shows the effusion and the signs that support it.
findings: Find the effusion first in the subcostal four chamber or parasternal long axis view.
Watch the right atrial wall in late diastole, just before the ventricles contract. Inward collapse of the right atrium is an early sign.
Watch the RV free wall in early diastole. Diastolic collapse of the RV is a more specific sign.
In the subcostal IVC view, a dilated IVC that barely changes with breathing supports a high right atrial pressure.
Watch the septum shift toward the LV with inspiration and back with expiration, a sign of exaggerated interdependence between the ventricles.
Doppler of mitral and tricuspid inflow shows exaggerated respiratory variation, the echo partner of pulsus paradoxus.
In a large effusion the whole heart may swing within the sac.
significance: Tamponade is an emergency treated by draining the fluid. The decision rests on the clinical picture, such as low blood pressure, raised venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus, with echo confirming the effusion and guiding drainage.
pearls: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis. Chamber collapse on echo supports it but does not prove it alone.
A small effusion that collects quickly, as after cardiac surgery or a perforation, can cause tamponade. Loculated fluid may compress only one chamber.
Chamber collapse may be absent when right heart pressures are already high, as in pulmonary hypertension.
mimics: Massive pulmonary embolism, which also causes shock with a dilated IVC
sources: Adler Y et al. 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases. Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921-2964. PMID 26320112.
Klein AL et al. ASE clinical recommendations for multimodality cardiovascular imaging of patients with pericardial disease. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013;26:965-1012. PMID 23998693.

Mukherjee M et al. Guidelines for the Echocardiographic Assessment of the Right Heart in Adults and Special Considerations in Pulmonary Hypertension: Recommendations from the American Society of Echocardiography. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2025;38:141-186. doi:10.1016/j.echo.2025.01.006.

name: Dilated cardiomyopathy
summary: A heart muscle disease with a dilated LV and reduced systolic function that is not explained by coronary disease or abnormal loading such as valve disease or hypertension.
findings: In the parasternal long axis, the LV cavity is large and more spherical than the normal bullet shape.
The walls are of normal or reduced thickness and thicken poorly in systole.
Wall motion is reduced throughout, usually without the sharp regional pattern of a single coronary territory.
The anterior mitral leaflet opens only a short way in diastole, leaving a wide gap between it and the septum.
The mitral leaflets may be pulled toward the apex and fail to meet in systole, causing secondary mitral regurgitation.
Check the left atrium and the RV, which are often enlarged as well.
Search the apex for thrombus in the slowly moving cavity.
significance: Systolic dysfunction drives heart failure, arrhythmia and thromboembolic risk. Echo measures the ejection fraction that guides treatment and should prompt a search for causes such as ischemia, valve disease, toxins and inherited disease.
pearls: Measure ejection fraction with the biplane method of disks from the apical four and two chamber views, avoiding foreshortening.
Ischemic cardiomyopathy can look the same. A regional pattern or thin, bright scarred segments favor coronary disease.
Secondary mitral regurgitation here is a disease of the ventricle, not the leaflets.
mimics: Athlete's heart, with a large but normally contracting LV
Severe aortic or mitral regurgitation causing LV dilation
sources: Arbelo E et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies. Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503-3626. PMID 37622657.
Lang RM et al. Recommendations for Cardiac Chamber Quantification by Echocardiography in Adults. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2015;28:1-39. PMID 25559473.

name: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
summary: An inherited heart muscle disease with LV wall thickening that is not explained by loading conditions such as hypertension or aortic stenosis.
findings: In the parasternal long axis, look for a septum that is thicker than the inferolateral wall.
In adults, clearly increased wall thickness in any segment, with no other cause, supports the diagnosis.
Scan every short axis level, because the thickest segment may be anterior, lateral or apical rather than septal.
Watch the anterior mitral leaflet in systole. Systolic anterior motion toward the septum narrows the LVOT.
The LV cavity is often small with vigorous systolic contraction.
In apical views, look for apical hypertrophy giving a spade-shaped cavity, which is easy to miss without careful imaging of the apex.
Doppler in the LVOT shows a late-peaking gradient when obstruction is present, sometimes only with provocation such as a Valsalva maneuver or exercise.
significance: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can cause sudden cardiac death, including in young people. Echo measures the wall thickness and outflow obstruction that guide risk assessment and treatment.
pearls: Measure wall thickness at end-diastole in the short axis at each level.
In a first degree relative of someone with the disease, or in a carrier of a disease-causing gene variant, a smaller increase in wall thickness can support the diagnosis.
Contrast helps when the apex is poorly seen.
sources: Ommen SR et al. 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for the Management of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy. Circulation 2024;149:e1239-e1311. PMID 38718139.
Arbelo E et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies. Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503-3626. PMID 37622657.

name: RV pressure overload
summary: A pattern where high pressure in the pulmonary circulation strains the RV, as in acute pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension.
findings: In the apical four chamber view, the RV looks as large as or larger than the LV and may form the apex.
In the parasternal short axis, the septum flattens and the LV becomes D-shaped.
Note when the septum flattens. Flattening in both systole and diastole points to pressure overload, while flattening only in diastole points to volume overload.
The RV free wall contracts poorly. In acute pulmonary embolism the free wall may be akinetic while the RV apex still contracts, the McConnell sign.
In chronic pressure overload the RV free wall thickens. It is best measured in the subcostal view at end-diastole.
The right atrium and IVC are often dilated.
Doppler of tricuspid regurgitation estimates RV systolic pressure.
significance: RV dysfunction is a strong marker of risk in pulmonary embolism and pulmonary hypertension. Seeing it at the bedside can change urgent management.
pearls: A thin-walled dilated RV suggests an acute process, while a thick-walled RV suggests a chronic one.
Judge RV size in an RV-focused apical view, because small rotation errors can make the RV look small or large.
The McConnell sign supports pulmonary embolism but is not specific and can also be seen in RV infarction.
mimics: RV volume overload, such as an atrial septal defect
sources: Mukherjee M et al. Guidelines for the Echocardiographic Assessment of the Right Heart in Adults and Special Considerations in Pulmonary Hypertension: Recommendations from the American Society of Echocardiography. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2025;38:141-186. doi:10.1016/j.echo.2025.01.006.
Lang RM et al. Recommendations for Cardiac Chamber Quantification by Echocardiography in Adults. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2015;28:1-39. PMID 25559473.

name: Mitral regurgitation
summary: Backflow from the LV into the left atrium during systole. It is primary when the valve itself is diseased and secondary when a diseased ventricle or atrium pulls the leaflets apart.
findings: In the parasternal long axis, check whether the leaflet tips meet in systole.
Look for a leaflet cause such as prolapse, a flail segment, thickening or a vegetation.
A flail leaflet whose tip points into the left atrium in systole is a specific sign of severe regurgitation.
If the leaflets look normal but are pulled toward the apex and fail to meet, suspect secondary regurgitation from a dilated or poorly moving LV.
Look at the size of the left atrium and the LV. Chronic severe regurgitation enlarges both.
Color Doppler in apical and parasternal views shows the jet. The width of its narrowest neck at the valve, the vena contracta, is a key sign of severity.
significance: Severity and mechanism decide whether repair or replacement is needed. Echo shows which leaflet is at fault and how well the LV is coping.
pearls: Do not grade severity on jet area alone. Eccentric jets that hug the atrial wall look smaller than they are.
In the ASE recommendations, a vena contracta of 0.7 cm or more is specific for severe regurgitation.
The jet usually points away from a prolapsing leaflet, so posterior leaflet prolapse sends the jet along the anterior side of the left atrium.
mimics: Trace regurgitation seen in many normal hearts
Aortic regurgitation jet in the LVOT
Normal pulmonary venous inflow into the left atrium
sources: Zoghbi WA et al. Recommendations for Noninvasive Evaluation of Native Valvular Regurgitation. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2017;30:303-371. PMID 28314623.
Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227. PMID 33332150.

name: Mitral stenosis
summary: Narrowing of the mitral orifice, most often from rheumatic heart disease. The LV fills poorly and the left atrium enlarges behind the obstruction.
findings: In the parasternal long axis, the leaflets are thickened and their tips open poorly in diastole.
The anterior leaflet domes into the LV in diastole, giving a hockey stick shape.
The posterior leaflet moves little and may be drawn forward with the anterior leaflet.
In the parasternal short axis at the mitral level, the orifice is a small fish mouth with fused commissures.
Tracing the smallest orifice in that view, called planimetry, measures the valve area directly.
The left atrium is enlarged. Look inside it for swirling smoke-like echoes or thrombus.
Doppler of mitral inflow shows a raised gradient and helps estimate the valve area.
significance: Severe stenosis raises left atrial and pulmonary pressures, causing breathlessness and atrial fibrillation. In the 2020 ACC/AHA valve guideline, a valve area of 1.5 cm² or less marks severe rheumatic stenosis.
pearls: Fused commissures are the hallmark of rheumatic disease.
Calcific stenosis in older patients starts at the annulus and spreads into the leaflet bases, without fused commissures.
Gradients rise with heart rate, so always note the rate with the gradient.
mimics: Left atrial myxoma obstructing the valve
High flow across a normal valve, as in severe mitral regurgitation
sources: Baumgartner H et al. Echocardiographic assessment of valve stenosis: EAE/ASE recommendations for clinical practice. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2009;22:1-23. PMID 19130998.
Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227. PMID 33332150.

name: Aortic stenosis
summary: Narrowing of the aortic valve opening, most often from calcification of a three-cusp valve in older adults or of a bicuspid valve in younger ones.
findings: In the parasternal long axis, the cusps are thick and bright with calcium and open poorly in systole.
In the parasternal short axis at the aortic level, count the cusps and see how far they open in systole.
A bicuspid valve opens as a fish mouth with only two commissures.
The LV walls are often thickened in response to the pressure load.
Judge LV function, because a weak LV can make a severely narrowed valve show only low gradients.
Continuous wave Doppler through the valve, often from the apical five chamber view, measures peak velocity and mean gradient.
significance: Severe aortic stenosis with symptoms carries a poor outlook without valve replacement. Severe stenosis is usually defined by a peak velocity of 4 m/s or more or a mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more.
pearls: Grade severity by Doppler and valve area, not by how bright the valve looks.
A Doppler beam that is not parallel to the jet underestimates velocity, so sample from several windows.
Low gradient stenosis with a reduced ejection fraction may need a dobutamine study to tell true severe stenosis from a weak ventricle that cannot open the valve fully.
mimics: Aortic sclerosis, with thickening but no obstruction
sources: Baumgartner H et al. Recommendations on the Echocardiographic Assessment of Aortic Valve Stenosis. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2017;30:372-392. PMID 28385280.
Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227. PMID 33332150.

name: Aortic regurgitation
summary: Backflow from the aorta into the LV during diastole, caused by disease of the cusps or dilation of the aortic root.
findings: In the parasternal long axis, check whether the cusps meet fully in diastole and measure the aortic root.
Look for a cause such as a bicuspid valve, cusp prolapse, a vegetation or a dilated root.
The jet may strike the anterior mitral leaflet and make it flutter in diastole.
Chronic severe regurgitation dilates the LV.
Color Doppler in the long axis shows the jet in the LVOT. Its width compared with the LVOT and its vena contracta help grade it.
Doppler of the descending aorta from the suprasternal view showing prominent reversed flow throughout diastole is a specific sign of severe regurgitation.
significance: Severe regurgitation loads the LV with volume, and surgery is timed to symptoms, LV size and LV function. Acute severe regurgitation, from dissection or endocarditis, is an emergency.
pearls: In the ASE recommendations, a vena contracta over 0.6 cm or a jet width of 65 percent or more of the LVOT points to severe regurgitation.
Always look at the aortic root and ascending aorta, because a dilated aorta is a common cause.
Acute severe regurgitation may show a normal sized LV with early closure of the mitral valve.
mimics: Trace regurgitation seen in normal hearts
Turbulent LVOT flow from outflow obstruction
sources: Zoghbi WA et al. Recommendations for Noninvasive Evaluation of Native Valvular Regurgitation. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2017;30:303-371. PMID 28314623.
Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227. PMID 33332150.

name: Mitral valve prolapse
summary: Billowing of one or both mitral leaflets above the annulus into the left atrium during systole, usually from myxomatous valve disease.
findings: Use the parasternal long axis and picture a line joining the two hinge points of the mitral annulus.
In systole, a leaflet that moves 2 mm or more above that line into the left atrium is prolapsing.
Look at leaflet thickness. Myxomatous leaflets look thick, long and redundant.
Note which leaflet is involved. The posterior leaflet is often affected.
Check for a flail segment whose tip turns into the left atrium, which suggests ruptured chords.
Color Doppler shows late systolic or holosystolic regurgitation, usually aimed away from the prolapsing leaflet.
significance: Most people with prolapse do well, but it is a leading cause of primary mitral regurgitation needing surgery. A flail leaflet usually means severe regurgitation.
pearls: Do not diagnose prolapse from the apical four chamber view alone. The saddle shaped annulus can make normal leaflets look as if they prolapse there.
Barlow disease involves both leaflets with marked excess tissue.
mimics: Normal leaflets in an off-axis apical view
Flail leaflet from papillary muscle rupture
sources: Zoghbi WA et al. Recommendations for Noninvasive Evaluation of Native Valvular Regurgitation. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2017;30:303-371. PMID 28314623.
Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227. PMID 33332150.

name: Infective endocarditis
summary: Infection of the inner lining of the heart, usually on a valve. Echo looks for vegetations and the damage they cause.
findings: Search the low pressure side of each valve, which is the atrial side of the mitral and tricuspid valves and the LVOT side of the aortic valve.
A vegetation is an irregular mass attached to a leaflet that moves on its own, out of step with the valve.
Sweep through several views, because a vegetation may show in only one plane.
Look for valve destruction, such as a perforation or a flail leaflet, and for new regurgitation on color Doppler.
Look around the aortic root for a thickened or echo-free space that may be an abscess.
Check the right sided valves, especially the tricuspid valve, in people who inject drugs.
significance: Echo findings are a major diagnostic criterion and reveal complications that may need surgery. Transesophageal echo is more sensitive. It is used when transthoracic images are negative or unclear but suspicion stays high, and it helps when a prosthetic valve limits the transthoracic view.
pearls: A normal transthoracic echo does not exclude endocarditis.
Larger vegetations, especially mobile ones, are thought to carry a higher risk of embolism.
Compare with earlier studies, because old healed vegetations and degenerative nodules can look alike.
sources: Delgado V et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis. Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948-4042. PMID 37622656.

name: Left ventricular thrombus
summary: A blood clot in the LV, usually at an akinetic or aneurysmal apex after an anterior infarct, or in a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle.
findings: Look at the LV apex in the apical four and two chamber views with reduced depth and a zoomed image.
A thrombus is a mass with a clear edge, distinct from the endocardium, sitting over a wall that moves poorly.
It may be flat and layered along the wall or bulge into the cavity and move.
Confirm it in at least two views and through the whole cardiac cycle.
Check the wall underneath. A mass over normally contracting muscle is unlikely to be thrombus.
Adjust focus to the apex and consider contrast when near-field clutter hides it.
significance: LV thrombus can embolise and cause stroke, so finding it usually leads to anticoagulation. Cardiac MRI is more sensitive than echo when the answer is uncertain.
pearls: Foreshortened views miss the true apex, where most thrombi sit.
Protruding and mobile thrombi are thought to carry a higher risk of embolism than flat layered ones.
Trabeculations and false tendons cross the cavity or follow the wall and are not clot.
sources: Levine GN et al. Management of Patients at Risk for and With Left Ventricular Thrombus: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association. Circulation 2022;146:e205-e223. PMID 36106537.
Lang RM et al. Recommendations for Cardiac Chamber Quantification by Echocardiography in Adults. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2015;28:1-39. PMID 25559473.

name: Regional wall motion abnormality
summary: Reduced movement and thickening of part of the LV wall, most often from ischemia or infarction in one coronary territory.
findings: Start in the parasternal short axis at the papillary muscle level, where all three coronary territories are seen at once.
Watch each segment thicken inward in systole. Thickening is more reliable than motion, because a segment can be pulled along by its neighbors.
Grade each segment as normal, hypokinetic, akinetic or dyskinetic.
Use the apical four, two and three chamber views to see every LV segment from base to apex.
Match abnormal segments to a coronary territory. The LAD supplies the anterior wall, anterior septum and apex, the right coronary the inferior wall, and the circumflex the lateral walls.
A thin, bright segment that does not thicken suggests an old infarct with scar.
Look for complications such as thrombus, aneurysm, ventricular septal rupture and mitral regurgitation.
significance: A new regional abnormality in someone with chest pain supports myocardial ischemia. Its location points to the culprit artery and its extent relates to prognosis.
pearls: Coronary territories vary between people, especially at the apex and the inferolateral wall.
Left bundle branch block, pacing and the septum after heart surgery can move abnormally without ischemia.
An aneurysm is a thinned, dilated segment, so its outward bulge is still there in diastole.
mimics: Left bundle branch block or a paced rhythm
sources: Lang RM et al. Recommendations for Cardiac Chamber Quantification by Echocardiography in Adults. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2015;28:1-39. PMID 25559473.
Mitchell C et al. Guidelines for Performing a Comprehensive Transthoracic Echocardiographic Examination in Adults. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2019;32:1-64. PMID 30282592.

name: Takotsubo syndrome
summary: Sudden and usually reversible LV dysfunction, often triggered by physical or emotional stress and most common in older women. It closely mimics an acute coronary syndrome.
findings: In the apical four and two chamber views, the mid and apical segments move poorly while the base contracts strongly.
The apex balloons outward in systole, giving the shape of a Japanese octopus pot.
The abnormal area usually extends beyond the territory of a single coronary artery.
Look for less common patterns, such as mid-ventricular, basal or focal forms.
The strongly contracting base can narrow the LVOT, sometimes with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.
Check the RV, which is involved in some patients, and the apex for thrombus.
significance: Takotsubo needs coronary angiography to exclude infarction, because the two can look alike. Function usually recovers, which a follow-up echo confirms.
pearls: Poor wall motion that reaches beyond the territory of one coronary artery, often all the way around the apex, favors takotsubo over an infarct.
Look for LVOT obstruction and report it, because it changes treatment.
Recovery on a follow-up study supports the diagnosis.
mimics: Anterior infarction from an LAD that wraps around the apex
sources: Ghadri JR et al. International Expert Consensus Document on Takotsubo Syndrome (Part I). Eur Heart J 2018;39:2032-2046. PMID 29850871.
Lang RM et al. Recommendations for Cardiac Chamber Quantification by Echocardiography in Adults. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2015;28:1-39. PMID 25559473.
